title: Anchor the measurement space: the per-filter cost is computed in coordinates the adversary itself controls, so the ruler drifts while it is used.
one_liner: A genuine concern about the moving-target measurement space, but it is a downstream design refinement (fixed reference space, frozen backbone) that assumes the mechanism is real; it does not adjudicate the idea's central unverified claim.
description: The per-filter k-NN cost is only as meaningful as the filter space it is measured in, and that space is co-trained with the generator: every discriminator update changes the geometry in which real-vs-fake distances are computed, so the generator can lower per-filter costs by steering the filters into configurations that make distances small rather than by matching the data. The moving-target problem is thereby relocated from the global divergence to the per-filter embedding, and the finite-ness of the cost buys nothing. What must change is an anchor: compute costs in a fixed reference space (frozen filters, a pretrained backbone, or input-space neighborhoods) with per-filter normalization calibrated on a fixed batch, so the ruler does not change while it grades the generator. The open question is whether the collapse the monitor flags is support non-overlap or an artifact of a drifting measurement space.

sections.technique: For each discriminator filter f, collect activation vectors on the real batch and the fake batch, and define a per-filter cost as the mean k-th-nearest-neighbor distance from fake activations to real activations — an empirical quantity that is finite even when the two supports are disjoint low-dimensional manifolds. The discriminator maximizes the sum of per-filter costs and the generator minimizes it, replacing the single global divergence. A support-collapse monitor tracks, per filter, the nearest-neighbor cost over time together with the periodicity of the filter's activations (autocorrelation peak at lag > 1); a filter whose cost is growing while its activations become periodic is flagged as collapsed, and its input weights are frozen or re-seeded instead of being left to oscillate. Compare against a WGAN-GP / spectral-normalization baseline on a setup where partial filter collapse is observed only after long training, and test whether per-filter costs stop the collapse earlier.
open_questions: Whether per-filter costs saturate toward zero as batches converge, letting a sum objective be satisfied by easy filters while others go silent and evade the periodicity monitor — and whether rank-based/scale-normalized costs plus a silence detector fix this.
Whether the oscillation-is-support-non-overlap claim can be distinguished from generic adversarial limit cycles, via a near-optimal-critic-per-step control experiment.
Unchanged from before: differentiability of k-NN, which network's filters collapse, and whether collapse is contagious across filters.
sections.rationale: My stance: the field treats gap B as a loss-design problem (pick a divergence defined on disjoint supports, e.g. Wasserstein) and gap A as a leftover dynamics problem (regularize or renormalize), and the load-bearing premise is that a single global scalar divergence is the right unit of training signal. I relax that premise by making the signal per-filter and empirically finite, and I invert the direction of explanation: oscillation is not the thing to suppress, it is the observable signature of the low-dimensional-support degeneracy, so one mechanism addresses both gaps. This is not a dismissal of WGAN — it identifies the one premise (global scalar loss) doing the work and shows what becomes possible once it is dropped: collapse can be detected and stopped per filter before it spreads, using the instability itself as signal. Unverified claims: that the observed oscillating collapse is specifically caused by degenerate gradients in non-overlapping regions, and that per-filter k-NN costs remain trainable at scale; both are hypotheses the experiment would test, not facts I have established.
sections.origin: Branch 1 is the decisive branch: it supplies a concrete falsification experiment (train with a near-optimal critic so gradients are fully informative, then check whether per-filter oscillation persists) that tests the idea's own load-bearing inversion — oscillation as the signature of support non-overlap — which the idea itself flags as its central unverified claim. Branch 0 raises a real concern about the co-trained measurement space drifting, but it presumes the mechanism holds and is a technique refinement that matters only downstream of the mechanism question.

nodes.text:
The oscillation is the message: per-filter support tracking instead of a global divergence
Filter collapse is not a leftover dynamics bug to regularize after fixing the loss — it is the generator discovering the region where the global JS/KL objective degenerates on low-dimensional supports, so the fix is per-filter, empirically finite training signals, not another divergence.
The paper's two gaps are one gap. The load-bearing assumption is that the right training signal is a single global divergence between two full distributions, and that the remaining collapse is an independent dynamics problem to be regularized away once the divergence is fixed. But the remaining collapse appears exactly where the global divergence goes degenerate on low-dimensional supports: a subset of filters stops receiving informative gradient, and their dynamics are then governed by residual optimizer noise, which shows up as oscillation. Instead of swapping in yet another globally-defined distance, drop the global scalar: give each filter a training signal that is locally defined and always finite because it is computed on the actual samples (k-NN style) rather than on assumed densities. The inversion is that oscillation is not a failure to suppress — it is the per-filter signature of support non-overlap, so the same mechanism that addresses gap B also diagnoses and stops gap A. Validation stops where the paper's method still collapses after long training; that is precisely the regime where the assumption must be dropped.

summary.accepted: carved from run_9472281b on acceptance: SlowCritic-WGAN: an EMA-gated temporal damper on a Wasserstein critic; The oscillation is the message: per-filter support tracking instead of a global divergence; FilterBank Sinkhorn: entropic OT over the joint (image, activation) distribution
open: Which side's filters collapse — the gap says 'a subset of filters' without naming the model; if the collapse is in the generator, the damper must move into the generator update and the composition changes.
Does damping the critic make it lag behind a fast-improving generator, and is a lag-1 autocorrelation detector sufficient to catch slower or aperiodic oscillatory modes?

Is a weight-EMA copy the right slow target, or should the target be an EMA of critic outputs on fixed anchors, since weight-space averaging across modes is not obviously equivalent to output-space smoothing?
How sensitive is the result to λ_t and gate hysteresis — too strong a damper could drive the critic toward a constant function and destroy the Wasserstein signal.
Are the original GAN paper's 'oscillating mode' failure and WGAN-GP's known oscillatory training the same phenomenon, or two different instabilities?
